title: Further Algebraic Fractions

findings.finding: Unchanged whole simplification tasks recur within and across exercises without an explicit retrieval purpose or a requested comparison between the copies.
findings.breakdown: The repeated eight-part exercise and the repeated individual parts supply identical expressions and decisions. Correct answers do not give these copies an instructional purpose.
findings.checked: Compared complete prompts and expressions. The eight parts of p16-q6 and p17-q10 match. The other matching groups are p5-guided-f-node/p11-q21-f/p16-q6-c/p17-q10-c; p15-q5-b/p17-q9-g; p14-q2-d/p18-q13-a; p31-q2-a/p31-q2-c/p32-q3-a/p32-q3-c; p31-q2-d/p31-q2-f; p31-q2-g/p31-q2-i; p32-q3-d/p32-q3-f; p32-q3-g/p32-q3-i; p33-q6-a/p33-q6-c; p33-q6-d/p33-q6-f; p33-q6-g/p33-q6-i; p33-q7-a/p33-q7-c; p33-q7-d/p33-q7-f; p33-q7-g/p33-q7-i; and p38-guided-a/p39-q2-f. Replacement answers were checked algebraically. Repairs change comparison groups together where necessary.
findings.assumptions: No explicit repetition purpose beyond the supplied material is assumed. Simplified answers retain the restrictions imposed by their original denominators.
findings.doneWhen: The identified unnecessary copies have different values, their replacement answers are correct, and the local denominator, sign and operation comparisons remain intact.

findings.finding: Extend the existing coefficient task with two nearby numerical cases.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up connects the surviving linear factor with the numerator's coefficients.
findings.checked: Expanding (x+3)(x-3), (x+3)(x-4) and (x+3)(x-5) gives coefficient pairs (0,-9), (-1,-12) and (-2,-15). All identities hold for x≠-3.
findings.assumptions: Expansion and coefficient comparison are available through the existing task.

repair.proposal: Treat the existing task as (a). Add (b) Find a and b if (x²+ax+b)/(x+3)=x-3 for all valid x. Answer: a=0, b=-9. (c) Find a and b if the quotient is x-5. Answer: a=-2, b=-15. (d) Across the quotients x-3, x-4 and x-5, how do a and b change each time? Answer: a decreases by 1 and b decreases by 3.

findings.doneWhen: The optional parts follow p20-q15 and retain its numerical coefficient-comparison method.

findings.finding: Use numerical side lengths to connect cancellation with constant rectangle area.
findings.breakdown: Students compare different rectangles whose side products remain equal.
findings.checked: For rectangle b, x=5 gives sides 2 cm and 1 cm; x=7 gives 1 cm and 2 cm; horizontal length 4 cm gives x=4 and vertical length 1/2 cm. All satisfy the geometric domain x>3 and have area 2 cm².
findings.assumptions: Substitution and solving a simple equation are prior knowledge.

repair.proposal: After p27-q12-c, add optional parts referring to rectangle b: (d) Find both side lengths when x=5. Answer: 2 cm and 1 cm. (e) Find both side lengths when x=7. Answer: 1 cm and 2 cm. (f) Find x when the horizontal length is 4 cm. Answer: x=4. (g) Explain why these three rectangles have the same area. Answer: [4/(x-3)]×[(x-3)/2]=2 cm².

findings.doneWhen: The follow-up uses the existing rectangle and separates each question into its own part.

findings.finding: Unchanged whole tasks recur without a stated retrieval purpose or a necessary comparison role.
findings.breakdown: The later copies repeat complete denominator and numerator decisions already required by identical tasks.
findings.checked: Compared complete instructions and expressions for every targeted copy. Retain p32-q3-a as the addition anchor for the immediate subtraction comparison in p32-q3-b. The other later copies have no supplied instructional purpose. All replacement answers below were checked algebraically.
findings.assumptions: Tasks are completed in booklet order.

repair.proposal: Retain earliest copies and p32-q3-a. Replace p31-q1-k with LCM of x²-16 and x+4, answer (x-4)(x+4). Replace the following Simplify tasks: p31-q2-c: 1/(x+1)+1/(x+5), answer (2x+6)/((x+1)(x+5)); p31-q2-f: 2/(x+1)+1/(x+4), answer (3x+9)/((x+1)(x+4)); p31-q2-i: 5/(x+1)+1/(x+2), answer (6x+11)/((x+1)(x+2)); p32-q3-c: 1/(x+1)+1/(x+6), answer (2x+7)/((x+1)(x+6)); p32-q3-f: 3/(x+1)-1/(x+2), answer (2x+5)/((x+1)(x+2)); p32-q3-i: 4/(x+2)-2/(x+1), answer 2x/((x+1)(x+2)); p33-q6-c: 1/(x+2)+1/(x+4), answer (2x+6)/((x+2)(x+4)); p33-q6-f: 4/(x²+5x+6)+3/(x+2), answer (3x+13)/((x+2)(x+3)); p33-q6-i: 3/(x²+5x+6)+1/(x²+4x+3), answer (4x+5)/((x+1)(x+2)(x+3)); p33-q7-c: 1/(x-5)+1/(5-x), answer 0; p33-q7-f: x/(x-2)+5/(2-x), answer (x-5)/(x-2); p33-q7-i: 6/(2-x)+3/(x-2), answer -3/(x-2). Retain original denominator restrictions in simplified answers.

findings.doneWhen: Unnecessary later copies have changed values and correct answers, while the immediate addition/subtraction comparison remains.

findings.finding: The example uses the multiplier 3x² without explicitly connecting it to the inner denominators.
findings.breakdown: The new compound-fraction method demonstrates applying the multiplier but leaves its selection unwritten.
findings.checked: p38-methods names the LCD, and p29 supplies prior LCM practice. Neither explicitly identifies 3x and x² as the denominators used to select this example's multiplier.
findings.assumptions: Algebraic LCMs are prior learning; calculator use is irrelevant.

repair.proposal: Before the multiplication line, add: 'The inner denominators are 3x and x², so their LCD is 3x².'

findings.doneWhen: The multiplier's origin is stated before it is used.

findings.finding: The compound-fraction examples combine factorisation, reciprocal division and cancellation without an opening rehearsal of those methods.
findings.breakdown: Identifying the main numerator and denominator does not rehearse changing division to reciprocal multiplication or factorising the resulting polynomials. Both displayed routes depend on these substantial earlier skills.
findings.checked: p13-method and p23-method supply the methods earlier. p37-identify-block rehearses structure only. The immediately preceding topic supplies LCD and addition work, but does not rehearse reciprocal division. The examples combine several earlier methods, warranting their rehearsal.
findings.assumptions: These methods have been taught previously. No calculator is needed.

repair.proposal: Before p37-identify-block add: (a) Factorise 3x²+x, answer x(3x+1). (b) Factorise 3x²−3, answer 3(x−1)(x+1). (c) Simplify (x²−1)/(x²+x), answer (x−1)/x. (d) Simplify (2/x) ÷ (3/x²), answer 2x/3. Answers apply wherever the original expressions are defined. Keep the review and identification activity within one page.

findings.doneWhen: Students rehearse the factorisation, cancellation and reciprocal-division steps before the examples combine them.

findings.finding: p39-q2-f repeats the complete simplification task from p38-guided-a.
findings.breakdown: The later task has unchanged signs, values and fraction structure, with no explicit retrieval or comparison purpose.
findings.checked: Compared both full prompts. Their expressions and instructions match.
findings.assumptions: Both tasks are completed in booklet order.

repair.proposal: Replace p39-q2-f with 'Simplify (1+3/x)/(1-2/x).' Answer: (x+3)/(x-2), with x≠0,2.

findings.doneWhen: The later task preserves its structure with different numbers.

findings.finding: Follow the parallel-resistor expression with numerical cases connecting equal resistances to half their individual resistance.
findings.breakdown: The existing context makes the effect of adding equal reciprocal contributions concrete.
findings.checked: For r=s=12, rs/(r+s)=6; for r=s=20 it equals 10. If equal resistors have combined resistance 9, each is 18. All values are positive and the denominators are nonzero.
findings.assumptions: Numerical substitution and simple linear reasoning are available by this topic.

repair.proposal: After p41-q8 append: (a) 'Find the combined resistance when r=s=12 ohms.' Answer: 6 ohms. (b) 'Find the combined resistance when r=s=20 ohms.' Answer: 10 ohms. (c) 'Two equal resistors have a combined resistance of 9 ohms. Find each resistor's resistance.' Answer: 18 ohms.

findings.doneWhen: The optional numerical parts follow the existing simplification and retain its physical context.

findings.finding: The exercise introduces deeper nesting together with a large outer division and a separate three-term algebraic fraction expression.
findings.breakdown: Earlier work supports two-variable fractions and individual operations, but students must now organise several levels of simplification simultaneously. No preceding task isolates simplifying a denominator that itself contains a fraction before taking its reciprocal.
findings.checked: p38-guided-d already supplies two-variable compound fractions, so two variables alone are not the gap. p45-q6 and p45-q7 develop ratio identities rather than deeper nesting. p47-q14 also combines nested expressions and several operations; it does not provide a small existing bridge suitable for reordering.
findings.assumptions: The supplied teaching is complete. Students know the individual operations; the sharp increase concerns their structural combination.

repair.proposal: Before p46-q13 add: 'Simplify, starting with the innermost denominator: (a) 1/(x−2−4/(x+1)); (b) 1/x−1/(x−2−4/(x+1)).' Answers: (a) (x+1)/((x−3)(x+2)), with x≠−1,3,−2; (b) −2(x+3)/(x(x−3)(x+2)), with x≠−1,0,3,−2. Part (a) introduces the extra nesting; part (b) adds only the outer subtraction.

findings.doneWhen: Students practise the additional denominator level before combining it with the full two-variable expression.

findings.finding: Use the same sum and product to calculate the sum of the squared reciprocals without finding x and y.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up connects the existing reciprocal sum with the cross term in its square.
findings.checked: Since xy=5, both reciprocals exist. Their sum is 9/5, giving 1/x²+1/y²=(9/5)²−2/5=71/25. The related expansion is also exercised in p44-q4.
findings.assumptions: Expansion of a squared binomial is prior learning.

repair.proposal: Relabel the existing expression in p44-q3 as part (a), then append (b): 'Using the same values of x+y and xy, find 1/x²+1/y².' Answer: 71/25.

findings.doneWhen: The follow-up remains attached to the numerical sum-and-product question and uses only available methods.

findings.finding: The opening review does not rehearse common-factor extraction before the examples combine it with quadratic and difference-of-squares factorisation.
findings.breakdown: The examples require extracting x from x²−x and 2 from 2x²+4x+2. These entry decisions are absent from the review's factorisation questions and its already-factorised cancellation tasks.
findings.checked: Common-factor extraction is established in p3-review-factorise and p4-guided-d. Although that is the preceding topic, these examples combine several earlier methods, so the mixed-method review exception applies. p12-review-a to p12-review-d do not rehearse extraction.
findings.assumptions: Common-factor extraction is prior learning. Calculator use does not affect this algebraic decision.

repair.proposal: Append to the existing 'Factorise' review: (e) 3x+12, answer 3(x+4); (f) x²−4x, answer x(x−4); (g) 2x²+10x+12, answer 2(x+2)(x+3). Keep the complete review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: The review rehearses numerical and variable common-factor extraction, including extraction before quadratic factorisation.

findings.finding: The Pythagorean construction requires students to invent both a general pair of odd denominators and a general hypotenuse in one step.
findings.breakdown: Adding the displayed fractions is supported, but proving the pattern requires two further modelling decisions: representing consecutive odd denominators and recognising a square for the sum of the resulting squared side lengths.
findings.checked: p43-q1 supports consecutive-integer representation and p43-q2 asks students to generalise an identity. Neither supplies the additional hypotenuse construction. p44-q3 and p44-q4 manipulate given relationships. The jump remains despite the exercise's challenge purpose.
findings.assumptions: Students know special products and Pythagoras' theorem. The obstacle is constructing the algebraic model, independent of calculator access.

repair.proposal: Append: 'Write the two odd denominators as 2n−1 and 2n+1, where n is a positive integer. After adding the fractions, compare the sum of the squares of the numerator and denominator with (4n²+1)².'

findings.doneWhen: Students have a route to the general side lengths while still performing the fraction addition and proving the identity.

findings.finding: Follow the reconstructed denominator with two numerical changes that test whether a common factor survives.
findings.breakdown: This connects cancellation to shared polynomial factors using the existing numerator and coefficient.
findings.checked: x²+8x+12=(x+2)(x+6), whereas x²+8x+7=(x+1)(x+7). The numerator is (x+2)(x+3). Both tasks use factorisation and cancellation already available by this topic.
findings.assumptions: Expressions are considered on their original domains.

repair.proposal: Append to p20-q16: (b) 'Keep a=8 and change b to 12. Simplify the resulting fraction.' Answer: (x+3)/(x+6), x≠−2,−6. (c) 'Keep a=8 and change b to 7. Can the resulting fraction be simplified by cancellation? Explain why.' Answer: No; (x+2)(x+3) and (x+1)(x+7) share no factor. Original domain: x≠−1,−7.

findings.doneWhen: The optional follow-up uses the existing question's numbers to distinguish similar-looking expressions from expressions with common factors.

findings.finding: Use part a to connect a zero combined numerator with two equal and opposite fraction values.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up gives a concrete interpretation of the numerator obtained during addition.
findings.checked: The combined numerator is 3x+11, so x=−11/3. This value is in the original domain. The first original fraction is −9/2 and the second is 9/2; the candidate's stated order was reversed.
findings.assumptions: Solving a linear equation and substituting into fractions are prior learning.

repair.proposal: Append to p36-q13: (g) 'For which value of x is the expression in part a equal to zero?' Answer: x=−11/3. (h) 'At this value of x, what is the value of the first original fraction?' Answer: −9/2. (i) 'At this value of x, what is the value of the second original fraction?' Answer: 9/2.

findings.doneWhen: Each follow-up part asks one question, and the original fractions' values are given in the correct order.

contextQuestions.question: Have students already learned that √((x-6)²)=|x-6|? The supplied teaching does not establish this, and the separate course titles do not establish whether it is available here. If it is unfamiliar, could the question specify x>6 so its side-length task uses the factorisation already practised?

notReliablyReviewed.reason: A term at the right edge of a later handwritten expansion is clipped. The first common-denominator line and the subsequent erroneous multiplication are visible, so the diagnosis above does not depend on reconstructing that term.

dropped.reason: Common-factor extraction is taught and practised in the immediately preceding simple-factorisation topic, including numerical and algebraic factors in p3-review and p4-guided-d. The immediately preceding-topic exemption defeats the claimed missing review piece; this continues that factorise-and-cancel method rather than synthesising several earlier booklet topics.

candidates.finding: The review asks students to ‘Factorise’ quadratics but does not rehearse extracting a common numerical or algebraic factor, which both worked examples use directly.

unchecked.reason: The handwritten image and alleged blue annotation were not supplied as visible evidence. The practice record supplies only an image reference and a correct textual answer, so the claimed erroneous annotation and mathematical transitions cannot be independently checked.

candidate.finding: The visible explanation 'They should have factorised before trying to make a common denominator' misdiagnoses a valid common-denominator step and misses the subsequent multiplication of numerator expressions that should be added.
